summary: prompt batch.pos, batch.n_seq_id, batch.seq_id left uninitialized — llama_batch_init uses malloc, auto-generation skipped because pointers are non-null
failure_scenario: llama_batch_init(n_tokens,0,1) allocates all arrays via malloc (not calloc). The code sets batch.token[i] and batch.logits[i] but never batch.pos[i], batch.n_seq_id[i], or batch.seq_id[i][0]. Because these pointers are non-null, llama.cpp's internal batch pre-processor (llama-batch.cpp:73-118) skips auto-generation. Garbage pos[] values feed wrong RoPE positions → garbled output. Garbage n_seq_id[] can cause OOB reads of seq_id[][] at line 60 of llama-batch.cpp (`s < batch.n_seq_id[i]`). This is the #1 most likely cause of the

summary: generation batch.pos, n_seq_id, seq_id left uninitialized on every decode iteration — same root cause as prompt batch
failure_scenario: Each iteration of the generation loop sets gen_batch.n_tokens=1, gen_batch.token[0]=new_token, gen_batch.logits[0]=1 but never sets gen_batch.pos[0], gen_batch.n_seq_id[0], or gen_batch.seq_id[0][0]. After the first generated token is decoded with garbage position, all subsequent KV cache operations use wrong positions. Every generated token after the first is corrupted. The old code used llama_batch_get_one which left all pointers nullptr, correctly triggering auto-position-assignment.

summary: llama_backend_init() called but never freed on error paths — missing llama_backend_free() before return on model-load failure and context-creation failure
failure_scenario: If llama_model_load_from_file() fails (line 46-50) or llama_init_from_model() fails (line 62-67), the function returns JNI_FALSE without calling llama_backend_free(). On a subsequent nativeInit call (e.g., from Settings retry), llama_backend_init() is called a second time with no intervening free. llama.h documents backend_init as "call once" — double init without free can cause undefined behavior (backend state corruption, memory leak, or crash).

summary: llama_sampler_chain_init return value never checked for null
failure_scenario: If memory allocation fails inside llama_sampler_chain_init, it returns nullptr. The subsequent llama_sampler_chain_add(sampler, ...) at line 165 dereferences the null pointer, crashing the process. On Android with memory pressure during model loading, this is a realistic failure mode.

summary: Exception catch block leaks gen_batch and sampler resources
failure_scenario: If any C++ standard library operation (e.g., std::string::append throwing std::bad_alloc) throws after lines 164/171 where sampler and gen_batch are allocated, the catch block at line 248 only releases promptStr but never calls llama_batch_free(gen_batch) or llama_sampler_free(sampler). Repeated generation under memory pressure leaks internal arrays and sampler chain state.

summary: batch.n_tokens uses first-pass probe count (n_tokens) instead of actual tokenized count (n_tokenized)
failure_scenario: batch.n_tokens = n_tokens at line 135 uses the buffer-size-probe count from line 108, not the actual number of tokens returned by the second llama_tokenize call at line 121 (stored in n_tokenized). If the two passes ever disagree (pathological input), trailing entries in tokens[] are 0 (BOS/UNK token from default vector init), injecting garbage tokens into the decode. Additionally, batch.logits[n_tokens-1]=1 at line 140 sets the logits flag on a potentially wrong index.

summary: TOCTOU race between modelLoaded check and modelMutex acquisition in generate()
failure_scenario: Thread A reads modelLoaded==true at line 91 (outside mutex) → Thread B calls unloadModel() (acquires modelMutex, calls nativeFree() freeing all C++ globals, sets modelLoaded=false, releases mutex) → Thread A enters modelMutex.withLock and calls nativeGenerate(). The C++ is_initialized guard catches the freed state and returns empty string, so no native crash — but the user sees a silent generation failure (returns null) with no clear error at the Kotlin level. Fix: re-check modelLoaded inside modelMutex.withLock.

summary: Null jstring passed to GetStringUTFChars causes undefined behavior
failure_scenario: If Java code calls nativeInit(null) or nativeGenerate(null, ...), GetStringUTFChars is invoked on a null jstring. The JNI spec does not define this behavior; it can silently produce null output, throw, or crash. Affects lines 33 (nativeInit) and 95 (nativeGenerate).

summary: Catch blocks only catch std::exception — non-std exceptions cross JNI boundary as UB
failure_scenario: All three try/catch blocks (lines 36-78, 98-251, 261-276) only catch std::exception. Non-std exceptions (e.g., a bare `throw` from undefined behavior, or Android-specific error structures) propagate past the JNI boundary uncaught, which is undefined behavior and typically kills the process. On Android, unexpected signals (SIGSEGV, SIGABRT from the native library) manifest as non-std-exception events that bypass these catches.

summary: withTimeoutOrNull wrapping blocking JNI calls provides no actual cancelability — the timeout is a billing illusion
failure_scenario: withTimeoutOrNull(LOAD_TIMEOUT_MS) and withTimeoutOrNull(GENERATE_TIMEOUT_MS) wrap nativeInit and nativeGenerate calls that run on Dispatchers.IO threads calling blocking C++ code. Kotlin coroutine cancellation on IO dispatcher uses Thread.interrupt(), but JNI-bound C++ code does not check Thread.interrupted(). The Kotlin timeout expires and returns null, but the native call continues running on the IO thread (holding both the Kotlin Mutex and the C++ g_llama_mutex) until the 90s C++ timeout fires. During this window, the IO thread is blocked and the Kotlin mutex is held by a zombie coroutine — no other operation (loadModel, generate, unloadModel) can proceed. Repeated timeouts exhaust the IO thread pool (64 threads), stalling all IO work.

summary: InputStream never closed when MIME type is unrecognized (else branch in importFile)
failure_scenario: When the resolved MIME type does not match text/plain, application/msword, or application/vnd.openxmlformats-officedocument.wordprocessingml.document, the else branch returns @withContext null without closing the InputStream opened at line 127. Each failed import leaks the underlying ParcelFileDescriptor (file descriptor). On older Android devices with 1024-FD limits, rapid repeated imports of unsupported file types exhaust FDs.

summary: readDocFile/readDocxFile resource leak when text extraction throws after document construction
failure_scenario: If HWPFDocument(inputStream).text (line 187) or XWPFDocument(inputStream).paragraphs processing (lines 201-202) throws an exception, doc.close() in the following line is skipped. POI 5.x removed deprecated finalize(), so GC does not reliably reclaim the backing stream. The underlying InputStream (and its file descriptor) leaks until the document object is finalized. Corrupted .doc/.docx files trigger this path.

summary: Missing llama_kv_cache_clear() between generations — stale KV cache from prior prompt bleeds into new generation
failure_scenario: If generate() is called twice (User A → summary → back out → User B → new summary), the KV cache from the first prompt is never cleared. The second prompt's tokens are decoded into the same cache, but residual KV entries from the first prompt (at different positions) can collide or pollute attention computations. This produces non-deterministic or degraded output on the second call. Fix: call llama_kv_cache_clear(ctx) before the prompt batch decode.

summary: isInitialized guard is dead code — it is set once in the init block and never cleared, providing no defense against post-unload calls
failure_scenario: isInitialized is set to true if System.loadLibrary succeeds in the init block. It is read at line 101 inside modelMutex.withLock. But unloadModel() calls nativeFree() which sets the C++ is_initialized=false — a completely separate variable. The Kotlin isInitialized is never reset to false, so line 101 always passes after a successful init. This gives a false sense of safety: it does not catch the case where the model was unloaded mid-use. The C++ side's is_initialized check is the real guard.

summary: importFile loads entire documents into memory with no file-size guard — OOM risk on low-RAM devices
failure_scenario: XWPFDocument constructs an in-memory XML model that can be 3-5x the file size. A 50 MB .docx with embedded images can consume several hundred MB of app heap. On devices with 256-512 MB heap limits, this causes OOM crash. No early-exit check on contentResolver.openFileDescriptor(uri)?.statSize is performed.

summary: withContext(Dispatchers.IO) placed inside modelMutex.withLock — suboptimal ordering increases lock contention
failure_scenario: Swapping the order to `return withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { modelMutex.withLock { ... } }` would release the mutex during the dispatcher switch. The current ordering holds the mutex across the thread-switch suspension point. Under concurrent generate() calls, the second caller blocks on modelMutex while the first caller is merely switching dispatchers — a pure scheduling delay, not actual work.

summary: Progress LOGI every 32 tokens (up to 8 log lines per default 256-token generation) clutters logcat
failure_scenario: Production logcat ring buffer on Android is limited (~256KB). Excessive progress logging evicts real error messages. The start and end timestamps already capture total generation time and throughput. Every-32-token logging should be gated behind a BUILD_TYPE debug check or removed once the pipeline is stable.
